```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Print results at most 60 characters wide, "#> " included, to fit a printed page.
options(width = 57)
# Keep the build machine out of printed query headers (load duckdb first, as it
# registers its own description when it loads).
loadNamespace("duckdb")
registerS3method("db_connection_describe", "duckdb_connection",
                 function(con, ...) "example database", envir = asNamespace("dbplyr"))
```

THIP's inpatient data are hospital records from claims paid through the
National Health Security Office (NHSO). This guide shows what is in them: which
tables there are, what one row means and which columns you will use most.

The map below is the whole guide in one picture: one table per fiscal year on
the left, and the groups of columns inside each table on the right.

```{r data-map, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# Inline, so the diagram travels with the page and keeps its title and description.
cat("```{=html}", "<div style=\"margin: 0.5rem 0 1.5rem;\">",
    readLines("figures/thip-data-map.svg"), "</div>", "```", sep = "\n")
```

Every example runs on the example database: a small set of invented records in
tables shaped like THIP's, with the same column names and text formats. The
records include a few values damaged on purpose, which later guides find. On
THIP, set up once as in [Start here](start-here.html), connect with
`thip_connect()` instead, and the same code works, apart from the differences in
[The example is DuckDB, THIP is
ClickHouse](database-from-r.html#the-example-is-duckdb-thip-is-clickhouse).

```{r connect}
library(thipR)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- thip_connect_example()
```

## One table per fiscal year

`thip_list_tables()` lists the tables you can read:

```{r tables}
thip_list_tables(con)
```

Each table holds one Thai fiscal year. Its name is `nhso` followed by the fiscal
year in the Buddhist era, and fiscal years run from October to September: fiscal
year 2567 is October 2023 to September 2024.

The example has three years. On THIP you will find tables from `nhso2560`
(fiscal year 2017) onwards, and separate tables of COVID-19 vaccinations.
`thip_list_tables()` hides tables whose names end in `_local`; if you see them in
another tool, they are storage pieces of the same data, so use the names without
`_local`.

## Point at a table

`tbl()` points dplyr at one table on the database. Behind the scenes, dplyr
hands the work to its companion package dbplyr; it comes with thipR, so you do
not load it yourself. We call the table `stays` and use it for the rest of this
guide:

```{r stays}
stays <- tbl(con, "nhso2567")
```

## Look at a few rows {.tabset}

The two tabs run the same query, one in dplyr and one in SQL; use whichever you
know. Without a sort order, which five rows come back can change.

### dplyr

```{r head}
stays |>
  select(age_y, sex, dateadm, datedsc, dischs, pdx, sdx1) |>
  head(5)
```

### SQL

```{r head-sql}
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT age_y, sex, dateadm, datedsc, dischs, pdx, sdx1
  FROM nhso2567
  LIMIT 5")
```

## A query, not a copy

`stays` is not a copy of the table in R. It is a query: R sends it to the
database each time you print it, and only the rows you print come back. That is
why the dplyr output starts with `# A query: ?? x 7`: the database has not
counted the rows. `show_query()` shows the SQL that dplyr writes for you:

```{r show-query}
stays |>
  select(age_y, sex, dateadm, datedsc, dischs, pdx, sdx1) |>
  head(5) |>
  show_query()
```

To bring a result into R as an ordinary data frame, end the pipeline with
`collect()`. Do that once the result is small: filter and summarise on the
database first.

## One row is one inpatient record

Each row is one inpatient record: a stay in hospital, with its dates,
diagnoses, procedures and discharge. Two columns identify things:

- `tran_id` identifies the record.
- `pid` identifies the person, as a hashed code: records with the same `pid`
  belong to the same person.

Both are hashed codes, so treat them as labels, never as numbers. The `…` in the
printout only means the value was cut to fit the page:

```{r ids}
stays |>
  select(pid, tran_id) |>
  head(2)
```

## One person, many records {.tabset}

People are admitted more than once, so counting rows counts records, not people.
First compare the two counts, then count each person's records and see how many
people have one, two, three and so on.

### dplyr

```{r people}
stays |>
  summarise(records = n(), people = n_distinct(pid))

stays |>
  count(pid, name = "records") |>
  count(records, name = "people") |>
  arrange(records)
```

### SQL

```{r people-sql}
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT count(*) AS records, count(DISTINCT pid) AS people
  FROM nhso2567")

DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT records, count(*) AS people
  FROM (SELECT pid, count(*) AS records
        FROM nhso2567 GROUP BY pid)
  GROUP BY records
  ORDER BY records")
```

## Every column is text

`thip_columns()` lists one table's columns and how each is stored:

```{r columns}
thip_columns(con, "nhso2567") |>
  head(8)
```

Every column is stored as text (`String`), including ages, dates and codes. Text
sorts character by character, so the largest age as text is not the oldest
person:

```{r text-age}
stays |>
  summarise(
    as_text = max(age_y, na.rm = TRUE),
    as_number = max(as.integer(age_y), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

As text, `"99"` sorts after `"102"`, because `"9"` comes after `"1"`. Three habits
follow from this:

- **Numbers:** convert with `as.integer()` before you compare them, as in
  `filter(as.integer(age_y) >= 65)`.
- **Codes:** keep them as text and compare with quotes, keeping leading zeros:
  `sex == "2"`, `health_region == "01"`.
- **Empty values** are usually empty text, `""`, rather than `NA`. Test for them
  with `== ""` or `!= ""`; [Check before you
  trust](data-checks.html#empty-values-and-ages) shows how to count both. When a
  column holds an empty value, the printout puts quotes around every value in
  that column, as in the `sdx1` column above.

Dates are text too, in two styles: `dateadm` and `datedsc` look like
`"20231015"`, while `death_date` looks like `"2023-10-15"`. Convert them before
you compare or subtract them; [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html)
shows how.

## The columns, by topic

The package includes `thip_fields`, a reference of the columns written from
THIP's data dictionary. These are the ones you will use most:

```{r key-fields}
key <- c("pid", "tran_id", "sex", "age_y", "dateadm",
         "datedsc", "dischs", "pdx", "sdx1", "proc1",
         "death_date", "health_region", "superdistrict")

thip_fields |>
  filter(field %in% key) |>
  select(field, description, format) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

To see every field, print `thip_fields` or open it with `View(thip_fields)`; the
`codes` column gives the meaning of each code.

## Diagnoses and procedures

Each record has one principal diagnosis, `pdx`: the main reason for the stay.
Up to 20 secondary diagnoses follow in `sdx1` to `sdx20`, such as long-term
conditions present at the time. THIP's dictionary lists these as ICD-10; Thai
hospitals code with ICD-10-TM, the Thai modification of ICD-10. The example
writes codes without the dot: `J189` is J18.9. Procedures, in `proc1` to
`proc21`, use ICD-9-CM.

The most common principal diagnoses in the example:

```{r top-pdx}
stays |>
  count(pdx, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8)
```

In the example, codes have three to five characters and no dot; [Check before
you trust](data-checks.html#the-shape-of-codes) shows how to find any that do
not.

Secondary diagnoses spread across many columns; the notebook platform also gives
`sdx_index`, which joins the non-empty ones into one text:

```{r sdx}
stays |>
  filter(sdx2 != "") |>
  select(pdx, sdx1, sdx2, sdx3, sdx_index) |>
  head(4)
```

To find the records with a condition, you search `pdx` and every `sdx` column;
[Flag conditions](condition-flags.html) shows how.

## Discharge and death

`dischs` records the patient's condition at discharge: recovered, improved, not
improved, dead, or a delivery or newborn outcome. `discht` records how they left:
with approval, against advice, by transfer and so on. Here are the `dischs`
values in the example, and what each code means:

```{r dischs}
stays |>
  count(dischs, sort = TRUE)

thip_fields |>
  filter(field == "dischs") |>
  pull(codes) |>
  strsplit("; ") |>
  unlist()
```

Most records end as 2, improved.

`death_date` is the date of death from death data linked to the person.
Before you treat a death as happening during a particular stay, convert both
dates (their formats differ) and compare `death_date` with `datedsc`.

## Where

`health_region` is one of Thailand's 13 health regions, written with two digits.
`superdistrict` is a group of districts in one province, which THIP uses instead
of single districts to protect privacy. THIP's dictionary gives it as the
location of the treating facility, so counts by super-district are counts by
place of treatment. To map super-districts to districts, boundaries or
populations, see [THIP Commons](https://songyosr.github.io/thip-commons/).

## In short

- There is one table per Thai fiscal year, named in the Buddhist era, running
  October to September.
- `tbl()` gives a query that runs on the database; only what you print or
  `collect()` comes into R.
- One row is one inpatient record; records with the same `pid` belong to the
  same person.
- Every column is text: convert numbers and dates, compare codes as text, and
  test empty values with `""`.
- Diagnoses are ICD-10 codes, in `pdx` and `sdx1` to `sdx20`.
- `thip_fields` describes each column and what its codes mean.

Next: [Working with a database from R](database-from-r.html). To run the code on
THIP, set up access first in [Start here](start-here.html).

```{r disconnect, include = FALSE}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```
